questions.question: In ascending binary search, `arr[mid]` is smaller than the key. Which update is correct?
questions.explanation: The midpoint and everything to its left are too small, so the next range starts at mid + 1.
optionFeedback: That searches the smaller half, where the larger key cannot be.
Correct: exclude the checked midpoint and the smaller half.
Keeping mid can repeat the same probe.
This keeps the wrong half and may repeat mid.

questions.question: What proves an inclusive binary-search range is empty?
questions.explanation: With inclusive bounds, low <= high means at least one candidate remains; low > high means none remain.
optionFeedback: low == high is a one-element range that still needs a probe.
Correct: the first possible index has passed the last possible index.
A midpoint of 0 can be valid.
A one-element array may contain the key.

questions.question: Why is binary search worst-case `O(log n)`?
options: Each probe removes about half the candidates
questions.explanation: The candidate count follows n, n/2, n/4, and so on until one remains.
optionFeedback: Correct: the number of halvings grows logarithmically.
Binary search assumes order; it does not sort.
The iterative version is also logarithmic, so recursion is not the reason.

questions.question: What extra space does the recursive version use that the iterative version avoids?
options: A sorted copy of the array
questions.explanation: Each recursive range occupies a stack frame, and there are logarithmically many nested calls.
optionFeedback: Neither version needs to copy the array.
Correct: halving creates O(log n) recursion depth.
No quadratic temporary structure is used.
The method stores indexes, not one object per value.
